theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A new supervisor at a Portmore distribution centre wants to earn her team's trust quickly. Which action matters most?
options: Promising pay rises she cannot approve
Doing what she says she will do, every time
Sharing gossip so that the team feels included
Avoiding all hard decisions in her first year

questions.stem: A manager lets his friend in the team pick the best shifts every month. What is the main effect on workplace relationships?
options: The team will work harder to become his friend
It has no effect as long as the friend works well
It shows strong and decisive leadership
Others see favouritism and trust falls

questions.stem: A team member tells her supervisor in confidence that she is going through a divorce and may need some time off. What should the supervisor do?
options: Tell the team so that they can offer support
Mention it in the staff newsletter
Keep it private and discuss support options
Ask her to keep her problems out of work

questions.stem: An employee asks his manager to keep a secret, then reveals that a colleague is being harassed. What should the manager tell him?
options: That some matters must be acted on, but discreetly
That every secret will be kept, whatever it may be
That he should report it to the media instead
That harassment is a private matter between staff

questions.stem: A hotel's new owners have set new service targets. How should the front office manager share them with her team?
options: Pin the targets on the notice board, no comment
Email them out and expect every staff member to read

questions.stem: A manager plans to change the office layout. Why should she consult the team before deciding?
options: Consultation removes all need for decisions
Staff often know practical problems and feel valued
The law requires a staff vote on every layout change
It lets her blame the team if the plan fails

questions.stem: Staff gave many ideas during a consultation, but only some were used. What should the manager do next?
options: Tell staff which ideas were used and why
Say nothing, since staff will see the changes anyway
Use only the ideas that came from senior staff
Ask staff not to send in ideas again in future

questions.stem: Which behaviour best shows active listening when a staff member raises a concern?
options: Checking your phone now and then while they talk
Planning your reply while they speak
Interrupting to give the answer quickly
Summing up what they said and asking questions

questions.stem: Why might a supervisor hold short, regular one-to-one meetings with each team member?
options: To check up on staff members' private lives
To replace all team meetings
To issue warnings in private
To build rapport and catch concerns early

questions.stem: A supervisor wants to give feedback on a staff member's rude reply to a customer. Which statement follows the situation-behaviour-impact approach?

questions.stem: A manager asks her team to be on time for meetings but often arrives late herself. What is the most likely result?
options: Staff will arrive earlier to make up for her
Punctuality in the team will improve over time

questions.stem: A purchasing supervisor often has disputes with the warehouse team over late orders. What would best improve the relationship?
options: Send all complaints through the general manager
Meet regularly to agree how orders are handled

questions.stem: Why should a supervisor build good working relationships with key suppliers?
options: To be given personal gifts at Christmas
To delay paying their invoices on time
To share the company's confidential information
To solve problems fast and get better service

questions.stem: A new operations manager lists everyone her team works with and rates each one's influence and interest. Why does she do this?
options: To decide where to focus relationship-building
To decide which people she should avoid at work

options: Accept it, as it builds the relationship
Accept it, but tell no one about it

options: Declare the link and stay out of the decision

options: Ignore it, because it happened outside work hours
Act under the conduct and social media policies

Staff helping each other on busy days

options: Her underlying interest
Her final position

questions.stem: Two team members bring a disagreement to their manager. What should she do first?

questions.stem: When handling a complaint of harassment, why should the manager keep careful, dated notes?
options: To share them with the whole team
For a fair process and an accurate record
To use against the complainant later

questions.stem: A staff member is unhappy with how her supervisor handled her complaint about shift allocation. What should happen?
options: She should simply drop the matter
The supervisor should decide again alone

questions.stem: Rumours about job cuts are spreading in a team and morale is falling. What should the manager do?
options: Ignore the rumours until they stop
Find out who started it and punish them

questions.stem: Half of a customer service team now works from home. What best keeps relationships strong?
options: Contact home workers only when problems arise
Hold every meeting in the office only

questions.stem: A supervisor disagrees with a decision made by her own manager. What is the most professional approach?
options: Raise her concerns privately, with reasons
Complain about the decision to her team

questions.stem: Which action best strengthens relationships in a busy team?
options: Praising only the top performer each month

questions.stem: A new team member is being left out of lunch breaks and group chats. What should the supervisor do?
options: Leave it, as people choose their friends
Order the team to include him at all times

questions.stem: Which source would best help a manager judge the health of relationships in her team?
options: The number of emails each person sends daily
A staff survey, plus absence and complaint trends
The colour scheme and layout of the office

questions.stem: In a team survey, 18 of 24 staff agreed that "my supervisor treats me fairly". What percentage agreed?
A department with an average of 40 staff had 6 leavers in a year. What was its staff turnover rate?
Formal complaints between staff fell from 12 last year to 9 this year. What is the percentage fall?
A supervisor realises she gave a team member wrong information that led to an error. What builds trust most?
options: Admit the mistake and help put it right
Blame the system that gave her the information
Say nothing, as the error is now fixed

questions.stem: Why should a manager apply workplace policies consistently to all staff?
options: So that she never needs to use judgement
So that staff see they are treated fairly
So that policies can be changed each week
So that friends can be given exceptions

questions.stem: Two members of a team strongly disagree about a new process. When is this kind of disagreement healthy?
options: When it becomes personal and loud
When one side is forced to back down
When it is about ideas and stays respectful
When it goes on for weeks unresolved

questions.stem: Relationships in a hotel team are suffering because everyone is overworked during the peak tourist season. What should the manager do?
options: Tell staff to keep their tempers in check
Cancel all breaks until the season ends
Hold a party but change nothing else

options: Avoid the subject so that it is not reopened
Move one of them to another branch

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term names a regular private meeting between a manager and one staff member to talk about work, progress and any concerns?
What term names a confidential counselling and support service, paid for by an employer, for staff with personal or work problems?
Two staff agree to let an impartial outsider help them talk through their dispute and find their own solution. What is this process called?
What word names a formal complaint made by an employee about their treatment at work?
What three-word term names the document that sets out the standards of behaviour expected of everyone in an organisation?
In a survey, 21 of 30 staff said that they trust their supervisor. What percentage is that?
A manager spends 6 hours of her 40-hour week dealing with disputes between staff. What percentage of her week is that?
What word names repeated, unreasonable behaviour at work that humiliates, intimidates or undermines a person?
What two-word term describes listening with full attention, summarising and asking questions to check understanding?
What word names the group of contacts, inside and outside an organisation, that a manager builds and keeps up for information and support?
What word names the trust and easy understanding between two people that makes communication flow?
What one word names the unfair practice of giving better treatment to some staff because the manager likes them personally?
In a dispute, what word names the demand a person states, as opposed to the need that lies behind it?
What word names an experienced colleague who is paired with a new team member to help them settle in?
What word names the duty to keep private information about staff secure and share it only with those who need to know?

essays.stem: Kerry-Ann has just been promoted to supervise the team she used to work in as a peer. Explain how she can build trust and confidence with the team in her first three months.
essays.modelAnswer: Kerry-Ann's relationship with her former peers must change, but it does not have to get worse. She should begin with a team meeting to acknowledge the change openly, explain her role, share the organisation's goals for the team and say how she intends to work. She should then hold one-to-one meetings with each person to listen to their views, their ambitions and any worries, especially with anyone who also applied for the job. Trust grows when she keeps her word, so she should make only promises she can keep and follow through. She must apply policies and allocate work fairly to everyone, and avoid any sign of favouritism toward old friends, while still being friendly. She should keep private matters confidential and stay out of gossip. Asking the team for ideas and acting on them shows respect for their experience. When she makes a mistake, she should admit it. She should also model the behaviour she expects, such as punctuality and courtesy. After three months she could ask for feedback on how she is doing.
markingPoints: Acknowledges the change of role openly and sets expectations
Listens through one-to-ones and consults the team
Keeps commitments and admits mistakes
Treats all fairly and avoids favouritism, keeping confidences
Models expected behaviour and seeks feedback

essays.stem: Two receptionists at a busy hotel front desk have stopped speaking to each other, and guests have noticed the tension. Describe the steps you, as their manager, would take to resolve the conflict.
essays.modelAnswer: I would act promptly, because the conflict is affecting guests and the rest of the team. First, I would meet each receptionist privately, at a quiet time, and listen without judging, asking open questions to understand what happened, how they feel and what they need. I would separate the facts from opinions and look for the underlying interests, for example a feeling that work is shared unfairly at shift change. Next, I would bring them together in a private room, set ground rules such as no interrupting and respectful language, and let each person explain their view while the other listens. I would summarise the common ground and the real issues, then ask them to suggest solutions, such as a clear hand-over checklist and a fair split of tasks. We would agree specific actions and write them down, and I would remind them of the standard of conduct expected at the desk. I would check in with both after a week and after a month. If the conflict continued, or involved bullying, I would use the formal policy or bring in a mediator.
markingPoints: Acts promptly and meets each person privately to listen
Identifies the real issues and interests behind positions
Holds a joint meeting with ground rules
Agrees and records specific solutions owned by both
Follows up and escalates to formal routes or mediation if needed

essays.stem: A call centre team of 50 staff shows these results. Agree that "I am treated with respect": 80% last year, 60% this year. Agree that "I can raise concerns safely": 70% last year, 50% this year. Formal grievances: 3 last year, 8 this year. Staff turnover: 10% last year, 22% this year. Analyse what the figures show and plan the actions you would take.
essays.modelAnswer: Every measure has worsened. Agreement that staff are treated with respect has fallen by 20 percentage points, from 80% to 60%, and agreement that they can raise concerns safely has also fallen by 20 points, from 70% to 50%, so half the team now feels unsafe speaking up. Grievances rose from 3 to 8, an increase of 5, which is more than double. Turnover rose from 10%, or 5 leavers, to 22%, or 11 leavers, out of 50 staff. Together these suggest a serious breakdown in relationships, perhaps linked to a change of supervisor, workload or the way people are treated. I would first find the causes by reading survey comments, studying the grievance themes and exit interviews, and holding small confidential group discussions led by someone neutral. I would share the results honestly with the team and promise action. Likely actions include training supervisors in respectful feedback and listening, regular one-to-ones, a clear way to raise concerns without fear, fair rosters and recognition. I would report monthly on progress and repeat a short survey after six months to check improvement.
markingPoints: Correctly states the 20-point falls in both survey measures
Correctly interprets grievances (up by 5) and turnover (5 to 11 leavers)
Draws a sound conclusion about relationships
Plans to find causes confidentially before acting
Plans practical actions with monitoring and a repeat survey

essays.stem: Explain why a manager should consult team members on decisions that affect them, and describe how to run a consultation and give feedback on what staff said.
essays.modelAnswer: Consulting staff before a decision brings in practical knowledge from the people who do the work, so the decision is usually better. It also shows respect, builds trust and makes people more willing to support the change, because they understand it and have had a say. In some matters, such as changes to working conditions, policy or the law may also require consultation. To run a consultation, the manager should first be clear about what is open for discussion and what has already been decided, so that expectations are honest. She should explain the issue and the reasons, give staff the information they need and enough time to think. She can use several channels, such as a team meeting, one-to-one talks and an anonymous form, so that quieter people can contribute. She should listen without defending her own view and record what is said. After deciding, she must report back: what was decided, which suggestions were used, and why others were not. Thanking staff for their input and reviewing how the change is working keeps them willing to be consulted next time.
markingPoints: Explains benefits: better decisions, trust and support
Is clear about what is open for consultation
Gives information, time and several channels to contribute
Listens and records views fairly
Reports back on the decision and how input was used

essays.stem: You have just become operations supervisor at a distribution company in Spanish Town. Plan how you would build and keep up a network of internal and external working relationships.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin by listing the people and groups my team depends on and who depend on us. Internally, these include my own manager, the sales, purchasing, accounts and human resource teams, and the drivers and warehouse staff. Externally, they include key customers, suppliers, transport contractors, security firms and local authorities. I would rate each by their influence and how much they are affected by our work, so that I focus first on the most important. In my first month I would arrange short introductory meetings with key contacts to learn what they need from us and what problems exist. With teams we hand work to, I would agree regular check-ins and clear ways of working, such as order cut-off times. With customers and suppliers, I would agree a main contact and review meetings. I would keep promises, return calls quickly and share information openly, while keeping confidential matters private and following the gifts and conflict of interest policies. Outside the company, I could join a professional association or business network. Every six months I would review which relationships need more attention.
markingPoints: Identifies internal and external contacts
Prioritises by influence or importance
Plans introductory meetings and regular contact
Agrees ways of working and keeps commitments
Maintains ethics and reviews the network over time

essays.stem: A team member's work has dropped and he seems withdrawn. Explain how you would handle a conversation with him, and when you would refer him to other support.
essays.modelAnswer: I would arrange a private conversation at a calm time, not in front of others, and open in a caring way, for example by saying that I have noticed he does not seem himself and that I am concerned. I would describe the specific changes I have seen in his work, without blaming him, and then listen carefully, using open questions and giving him time to speak. I would respect whatever he chooses to share and keep it confidential, except where someone's safety is at risk. If the cause is work-related, such as workload or a conflict, we could agree practical steps, like adjusting tasks for a while. If the cause is personal, such as health, money or family problems, I would not try to act as a counsellor. I would tell him about the employee assistance programme or other professional services, and about any leave or flexible working that policy allows. If he said anything suggesting he might harm himself, I would get urgent professional help at once. We would agree to meet again, and I would keep a brief, confidential note.
markingPoints: Private, caring opening based on observed changes
Listens with open questions and respects confidentiality and its limits
Agrees practical support for work-related causes
Refers personal problems to professional help such as the assistance programme
Recognises urgent risk and arranges follow-up

essays.stem: A team member tells you that a colleague has been bullying her for several weeks. Explain how you would respond, from the first report to the follow-up.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank her for telling me, take the report seriously and reassure her that she will not be punished for raising it. I would listen carefully, let her describe what has happened, when and where, and whether anyone saw it, and I would write dated notes. I would explain the organisation's bullying and harassment policy and the options, both informal and formal, and ask what she would like to happen, while making clear that serious matters may have to be acted on. I would check whether she needs immediate support, such as a change of shift or the employee assistance programme. Depending on the seriousness and her wishes, I might speak to the colleague, or I would refer the matter to human resources for a formal investigation. Throughout, I would treat both people fairly, keep information confidential and avoid prejudging the outcome, because the colleague also has a right to respond. Once the matter is settled, I would check in with her regularly, watch for any retaliation and take action on any lessons for the team, such as training on respectful behaviour.
markingPoints: Takes the report seriously and reassures against retaliation
Listens and records dated facts
Explains the policy, informal and formal options, and gives support
Acts or refers fairly, with confidentiality and a fair hearing for both
Follows up and watches for retaliation

essays.stem: Compare informal and formal ways of dealing with difficulties between staff, and recommend when a manager should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Informal approaches include a quiet word, a private conversation with each person, a facilitated discussion between them, or mediation. They are quick, flexible and less stressful, they keep relationships intact and they let the people involved find their own solution. Their weaknesses are that there may be no written record, the outcome cannot be enforced, and they may be unsuitable when there is a big imbalance of power. Formal approaches follow the organisation's written procedures, such as the grievance, disciplinary or bullying and harassment procedures. They include a written complaint, an investigation, a hearing, a decision and a right of appeal. They are fair and consistent, create a record and can lead to sanctions, which protects people when the matter is serious. However, they take longer, can make positions harder and may damage relationships. I would recommend trying informal methods first for most everyday disagreements, such as clashes over workload or communication style. Formal procedures should be used when the issue is serious, such as harassment, violence, discrimination or a breach of policy, when informal steps have failed, or when the staff member asks for a formal process.
markingPoints: Describes informal approaches with strengths and weaknesses
Describes formal approaches with strengths and weaknesses
Makes a fair comparison
Recommends informal first for everyday issues
Recommends formal routes for serious matters or failed informal steps

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can maintain good working relationships in a team where some staff work from home and some work in the office.
essays.modelAnswer: In a mixed team there is a risk that home workers feel left out and office staff feel they carry more of the load, so the manager must work at fairness and connection. She should agree team ground rules on working hours, response times, which tools to use for what, and when people are expected in the office. Regular contact is essential: short daily or weekly check-ins by video, team meetings in which home and office staff join in the same way, and one-to-one calls with each person. She should share information through the same channels for everyone, so that decisions are not made in corridor talk that home workers miss. Work should be allocated and judged on results, not on who is seen at a desk, and recognition should go to all. Some shared time in person, such as a monthly team day, helps build rapport. She should watch for signs of isolation or overwork in home workers and encourage them to switch off after hours. Finally, she should ask the team regularly how the arrangement is working and adjust it.
markingPoints: Recognises the risks of isolation and unfairness
Sets ground rules for communication and availability
Holds regular inclusive meetings and one-to-ones
Shares information and allocates and recognises work fairly
Supports wellbeing and reviews the arrangement

essays.stem: Explain why a manager must model the behaviour she expects from her team, and give examples of how she can show integrity, respect and fairness each day.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff watch what managers do more closely than they listen to what they say. If a manager breaks the rules she sets, her words lose force, staff feel that standards apply only to them, and trust falls. When she models good behaviour, she sets a clear standard and earns the right to hold others to it. She shows integrity by being honest, keeping promises, admitting her mistakes, declaring any conflict of interest and refusing improper gifts. She shows respect by greeting people, listening without interrupting, using a calm tone even under pressure, keeping private information confidential and never belittling anyone in front of others. She shows fairness by sharing out work, overtime and opportunities by clear rules, applying policies in the same way to everyone, giving credit to those who earned it and avoiding favouritism toward friends. She also follows the same rules on punctuality, breaks and safety that she expects of staff. Over time, these daily actions build a culture in which people treat each other well, and the manager has fewer conflicts to resolve.
markingPoints: Explains why modelling matters for trust and standards
Gives examples of integrity
Gives examples of respect
Gives examples of fairness
Links modelling to the team's culture and fewer difficulties

practical1.title: Resolve a conflict between two team members and agree a written resolution (role play)
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack about two made-up team members in conflict (for example two cashiers at a supermarket in Old Harbour who clash over break times, or two clerks at an insurance office who dispute who handles a difficult client), with separate role cards for each person and an extract from the organisation's conduct and grievance policies. Your group plans and acts out the full process in three stages: a private talk with each person, a joint meeting, and a follow-up talk a month later. Give each member a named role: manager (prepares the plan and leads all three stages), team member A and team member B (study their role cards and play them realistically), human resource adviser (prepares a one-page summary of the policy steps and advises the manager when asked), and recorder (writes the notes of each stage, the written agreement and the follow-up plan). In a group of four, the human resource adviser also records. After the role play, every member writes a short reflection on what helped and what made things harder. If time allows, swap roles and run a shorter second round.
materials: Case pack and role cards from the assessor
Extract from a made-up conduct and grievance policy
Note sheets, an agreement template and pens
A quiet room or screened area with a table and chairs
photos: The manager's written plan for the three stages
The private talks taking place, with the notes
The joint meeting with the ground rules shown
The written agreement signed by both team members
The follow-up plan and the human resource adviser's policy summary
checklist: Took a named role and prepared their part
The manager listened to each side, kept calm and stayed neutral
The real issues and interests were identified, not just positions
The agreement is specific, fair and owned by both parties
Confidentiality and the policy steps were respected
The follow-up plan says when and how progress will be checked
Reflected honestly on their own part
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not act out real conflicts between colleagues
Keep the role play respectful: no shouting, threats or personal remarks
Any member may step out of a role at any time if they feel uncomfortable
Keep the notes and reflections confidential to the group and the assessor

practical2.title: Map a team's working relationships and produce a relationship action plan
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up team (for example the front office of a guest house in Port Antonio, or the customer service unit of a courier company in Kingston), with a list of the people and organisations it works with, staff survey results for two years, grievance and turnover figures, and short notes from exit interviews. As a group, produce: a poster mapping the team's internal and external stakeholders by influence and interest; a spreadsheet chart comparing the two years' survey results, with the changes in percentage points worked out and checked twice; a one-page analysis of what the figures show; a consultation plan for discussing the findings with the team; a twelve-month relationship action plan with owners and dates; and a one-page draft of team behaviour standards. Give each member a named role: stakeholder mapper (poster), data analyst (chart and figures), analysis writer, consultation planner (consultation plan and team standards), and action planner (relationship action plan). In a group of four, the consultation planner also writes the analysis. Present the work to the assessor in ten minutes, with each member explaining their part.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: stakeholder list, survey results, grievance and turnover figures, exit interview notes
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
Flipchart or poster paper, markers and sticky notes
photos: The survey chart on screen with the changes worked out
The consultation plan and the draft team standards
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The stakeholder map is complete and sensibly placed
The figures and changes are correct and clearly shown
The analysis draws sound conclusions from the evidence
The consultation plan and standards are fair and respectful
The action plan is specific, realistic and has owners and dates
Explained their part clearly during the presentation
safety: Use only the made-up data and invented names
Treat survey comments and exit notes as confidential
Discuss the case respectfully; do not refer to real colleagues
Share the work fairly and take short breaks
